satisfied_inclusion_points: The study analyzes morphosyntactic concepts in Transformer-based language models (Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B).

It empirically assesses syntactic structure or knowledge by training probing classifiers on residual-stream activations from the model's middle layer to predict morphosyntactic concepts across languages.
It trains sparse autoencoders (Gated SAEs) to identify multilingual features encoding morphosyntactic concepts from the same transformer models.

It evaluates cross-lingual sharing and causal influence via attribution patching and feature ablations, reporting multilingual feature overlap (up to ~50%) and the reliance of probes on massively multilingual features.

It demonstrates functional selectivity through feature steering interventions in a machine translation setting, showing targeted concept manipulation with generally high selectivity and demonstrated cross-language applicability.
evidence_highlights: The models considered are Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B (Transformer language models).
Probing classifiers are trained for each morphosyntactic concept and language on residual-stream activations from the model's middle layer.
Gated SAEs are trained to discover multilingual feature directions for morphosyntactic concepts.
Attribution patching and ablations show that multilingual features drive probe performance and that a subset of features is shared across languages.
Machine translation experiments with feature steering demonstrate functional selectivity of the identified features.
decision_rationale: 全文直接證實 Stage 2 納入條件：使用 Transformer-based 語言模型進行語法概念的實證分析，透過探測分類器、SAEs、因果干預與跨語言實驗，評估語法知識的跨語言表徵及其可控性，且未出現排除條件所述的情境。故評為強納入。

satisfied_inclusion_points: The full text empirically analyzes syntactic knowledge in LLMs by using linguistic minimal pairs to probe internal representations.
The study measures activation differences across minimal pairs to quantify linguistic similarity, focusing on syntactic phenomena (e.g., Subject–Verb Agreement, Binding, NPI licensing).
The evaluation uses syntactic benchmarks (BLiMP, SLING, RuBLiMP) and reports an extensive, multi-language, large-scale analysis (100+ LLMs across three languages and 150k minimal pairs).
The work includes empirical analysis of how linguistic similarity aligns with theoretical categorizations and with semantic similarity, addressing core syntax-related interpretability questions.
The paper demonstrates cross-language analysis and language clustering patterns, evidencing empirical assessment of syntactic knowledge in LLMs across languages.
